GOVERNMENT OF THE PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF BANGLADESH REPRESENTED BY THE SECRETARY, MINISTRY OF POWER, ENERGY AND MINERAL RESOURCES, BANGLADESH SECRETARIAT, DHAKA AND OTHERS
full_judgment:
13. Although the question is raised by none we, for us, feel called to put on records the idea of "Property of the Republic" as envisaged in Art. 143 of the Constitution to be kept in mind while arguing, if ever, to exclude writ by reference to ordinary or commercial contract doctrine. We know of no case at the moment in which a contract touching upon "Property of the Republic" vis-a-vis Article 143 has ever been debated, before or decided as such by our superior court. Article 143 reads as follows: 

 143(I): (1) There shall vest in the Republic, in addition to any other land or property lawfully vested- 

 14. A bare reading of Article 143 clearly suggests, amongst others, that all minerals and other things of value underlying any land of Bangladesh are property of the Republic. The side note of .the Article is couched with the phrase "Property of the Republic". There are other properties lawfully vested in the Republic. But it is only minerals and other things of value underlying any land or ocean within our territorial waters or the ocean over continental shelf are given special treatment in the Constitution as property title to which is directly vested in the Republic. This to our mind means by necessary implication that minerals or other things of value underlying any land or ocean are public property of the kind which is directly owned by the state. It is the sense exploration, production, distribution, sale and management of the natural gas must of necessity have public element open to public law limitations regardless of form adopted to sell or otherwise dispense with the property.
